This article is based on the Douyin video “Episode 53 | The Story Behind the Ma Family Army!” by the creator Mystery Archives, published on November 9, 2026. Video link: https://v.douyin.com/BJpg3FPzn9U/

To break records, they were harnessed with ropes and dragged behind a three-wheeled motorcycle as they ran. To deliver results, they were injected with massive doses of performance-enhancing drugs.

In the 1990s, a group of Chinese girls swept the world's middle- and long-distance running events, smashing world records and stunning the globe. But no one could have imagined the dark story hiding behind the dazzling myth.

This is the story behind the Ma Family Army.

1. 1993: The Red Whirlwind in Stuttgart

In 1993, at the World Athletics Championships in Stuttgart, Germany, a red whirlwind swept through the women's middle- and long-distance events.

Wang Junxia, Qu Yunxia, and Zhang Linli took three golds, a silver, and a bronze between them. Later that year, at China's National Games, the track became their home turf: race after race, they broke Asian records, national records, and even long-standing world records — 66 records at all levels in a single year.

Wang Junxia's 10,000 meters in 29:31.78 shook the entire world of track and field.

Overnight, the Ma Family Army became national heroes, their faces in every newspaper. Their coach, Ma Junren, was lifted onto a pedestal. The media chased them everywhere, and even the Spring Festival Gala sent an invitation. Ma boasted that he could break whichever record he wanted, and that the world would have no rival for the next ten years.

To everyone watching, this looked like a miracle built on sheer hard work. Outsiders saw them on the podium, flowers in hand, flags draped over their shoulders.

But inside the closed training base was a cruelty most people could never imagine.

2. Ropes, Resistance Bands, and Needles

Ma Junren's training was brutally extreme. He rode a three-wheeled motorcycle with a resistance band tied to a running athlete — the moment she slowed, the bike dragged her forward.

Years of relentless overtraining left these teenage girls covered in injuries, their joints and internal organs under constant, enormous strain. The team lived under closed management, almost no freedom at all, every move strictly controlled.

But the darker secret lay in syringes and pills.

Starting in 1991, Ma Junren began giving his athletes banned substances. Often he administered the injections himself, following a dedicated doping schedule. During the high-altitude training camp in Qinghai, the doses reached their peak: what had once been one dose split among three athletes became one dose per athlete. Even on the train, en route, injections had to be arranged.

To reduce risk, he even ordered every athlete to have her appendix removed, and strictly forbade anyone from getting a medical checkup on her own. Anyone caught sneaking off for a checkup was scolded and beaten.

Long-term drug use caused irreversible damage. Many of the girls suffered constant liver pain, endocrine disorders, and severe menstrual irregularities.

The beatings, the exploitation, the pain from the drugs, and the fights over prize money piled up, little by little, into the fury that would finally break the team apart.

3. December 1994: The Mutiny

On December 12, 1994, the mutiny that shocked the nation erupted.

Led by Wang Junxia, more than a dozen core athletes — including Zhang Lirong, Zhang Linli, and Liu Dong — handed in their resignations together. Ma Junren talked with them through the night, trying to win them back, but their minds were made up. In the early hours of the next morning, while Ma was home resting, the girls quietly left the Dalian training base and walked out as a group, breaking with him for good.

The team fell apart overnight. Ma Junren sat on the rocks by the sea until dawn, several times thinking of taking his own life. Not long after, his father, hearing the news of the mutiny, died of a sudden attack brought on by fury and grief. On his way to the funeral, Ma was in a serious car accident and nearly died himself.

The once-glorious Ma Family Army collapsed in ruins.

4. The Joint Letter

After the mutiny, most people assumed it was just a dispute over prize money, a falling-out between coach and athletes.

It wasn't until March 28, 1995, that the truth came out: led by Wang Junxia, ten athletes signed a joint letter and delivered it to the writer Zhao Yu, accusing Ma of forcing them to take banned drugs for years and subjecting them to prolonged abuse. In the letter, they wrote in despair: “We are human beings, not machines — and certainly not livestock.”

In 1998, Zhao Yu's book The Ma Family Army Investigation was published. But its most important chapter — the 30,000-word exposé “The Drug Demon Strikes the Ma Family Army” — was forcibly cut. The sealed truth stayed buried for 17 years, until the book was reissued in 2016 with the full text restored, and the whole country was stunned.

Then, on the eve of the 2000 Sydney Olympics, several Ma Family Army athletes failed drug tests, and the entire team was barred from the Games. In 2001, two athletes were banned; Ma Junren received only a written reprimand.

The myth was nailed to the post of controversy for good.

5. The Price of the Myth

After leaving Ma Junren, the athletes refused to use banned drugs ever again. But they discovered that without the drugs, they could no longer reach their peak. Many of them, their bodies broken, ended their careers early — their youth and their health left behind forever in those training years.

Only Wang Junxia went on to win the women's 5,000 meters at the Atlanta Olympics, fulfilling her Olympic dream.

Looking back, the Ma Family Army is a deeply complicated symbol. Countless Chinese people wept with joy at those victories, longing for China to hold its head high on the world stage. But gold medals should never come at the cost of athletes' health. Sport is, at its core, about fairness and respect — not a false glory built on drugs.

Behind those once-cheered world records, behind the flowers and applause, was the terrible price paid by a group of teenage girls.

The myth is over. What it leaves for Chinese sport is a heavy lesson: fair competition, and reverence for life — that is what sport is truly supposed to be.
excerpt_en: In 1993, a team of teenage Chinese girls shattered world records and became national heroes. Behind the glory was a regime of forced doping, brutal training, and a coach who treated his athletes like machines.
title_en: The Ma Family Army: The Myth and the Drugs Behind It
